etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fleute, floute, flote, from Old French flaute, fleüte, from Old Provençal flaüt, of uncertain origin. Perhaps ultimately from three possibilities:

definitions.definition: (music) A woodwind instrument consisting of a tube with a row of holes that produce sound through vibrations caused by air blown across the edge of the holes, often tuned by plugging one or more holes with a finger; the Western concert flute, a transverse side-blown flute of European origin.

quote.citation: 1709, Alexander Pope, “January and May; or, The Merchant’s Tale, from Chaucer”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], published 1717, →OCLC, page 217:
quote.text: The breathing flute's ſoft notes are heard around, / And the ſhril trumpets mix their ſilver ſound; / The vaulted roofs vvith echoing muſic ring, / Theſe touch the vocal ſtops, and thoſe the trembling ſtring.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) A recorder, also a woodwind instrument.
A glass with a long, narrow bowl and a long stem, used for drinking wine, especially champagne.

quote.citation: 2018, Sally Rooney, “Six Months Later (July  2013)”, in Normal People:
quote.text: These are champagne glasses, says Peggy.No, I mean the tall ones, Jamie says.You're thinking of flutes, says Peggy. These are coupes.

definitions.definition: A lengthwise groove, such as one of the lengthwise grooves on a classical column, or a groove on a cutting tool (such as a drill bit, endmill, or reamer), which helps to form both a cutting edge and a channel through which chips can escape.
(architecture, firearms) A semicylindrical vertical groove, as in a pillar, in plaited cloth, or in a rifle barrel to cut down the weight.
A long French bread roll, baguette.[1]
An organ stop with a flute-like sound.
A shuttle in weaving tapestry etc.

quote.citation: 1895, S. R. Crockett, A Cry Across the Black Water:
quote.text: The green turf was velvet underfoot. The blackbirds fluted in the hazels there.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To utter with a flutelike sound.

quote.citation: 1960, P[elham] G[renville] Wodehouse, chapter XIII, in Jeeves in the Offing, London: Herbert Jenkins, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Oh, there's my precious Poppet,” said Phyllis, as a distant barking reached the ears. “He's asking for his dinner, the sweet little angel. All right, darling, Mother's coming,” she fluted, and buzzed off on the errand of mercy.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To form flutes or channels in (as in a column, a ruffle, etc.); to cut a semicylindrical vertical groove in (as in a pillar, etc.).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Compare French flûte (“a transport”)?, Dutch fluit.

definitions.definition: A kind of flyboat; a storeship.
